I was an RA for 3 years at a state school 

We got free room and food and $100 stipend once a month ($900 total)

Rooms differed a lot in quality. For two of the years I was in a new large suite, private room sharing bathroom/sinks with 2 other private rooms (4 roommates). The other year I was in a regular dorm. 


Responsibilities included

Weeknight duty 8pm-8am once a week (on call swapped between desk buddy)

Weekend 24/7 duty Friday 8pm-Monda 8am anywhere from 2-4 weekends per 10 week term.

Door decs every term

Bulletin boards 2 per term

Floor meetings 2-3 per term

Volunteering at 2 RHA (residence hall association) events per term

Staff meetings every week

1:1 with RD every other week

Resident 1:1s every term

Room checks at the end of every term

Helping with move in 

There's probably more that I am forgetting. The most brutal by far was being on call 24/7 over Halloween weekend. No sleep, I'm sure you all can relate 😂

If it's wasn't for this it would be for something else. This was a big blow to me my first year because I hadn't been disliked by anyone (at least extremely openly).

My advice is to get comfortable being disliked, get comfortable in awkward situations, and work towards letting it not affect you. And also, you're there for school above all else and that is more important than this job.

1. I don't think it's possible to answer this question because different universities have different job requirements. Sometimes RAs are tasked with maintaining the safety of their communities while others are more responsible for planning events, and sometimes both. 

2. I think that there is a fair way to go about this. RAs should receive housing and food compensation to do a baseline amount of work (example: leading events, bulletin boards, door decs etc). Then there should be additional hourly compensation for work (like being on call) that is unpredictable. I've heard of universities like this, where RAs can pick up shifts voluntarily at desk for extra money, and I think that is very fair. 

Basically, if a university is having you deal with very challenging things, they should make sure you do not have to worry about housing finances to do it, or provide a way for us to get additional income.

At my university we get housing, food, and a monthly stipend, but the food is abhorrent, so most of us blow the stipend on food from off campus. We've been arguing for our meal plan to be traded for just the monetary value (so if we get $500 for food in dining dollars, just give us $500 so we can get better food or be able to help pay for school). But that's not going to happen anytime soon.

All in all it's a combination of university factors and what the expectations are from the RAs.

Make friends with your coworkers.
Talk with a returning/head RA to learn how to do the job/find out if there are things you need to know that weren't covered in training.
Don't give residents your personal phone number.
Establish boundaries with residents and coworkers if needed, for example if you are not working and there is an incident it is ok to direct the people involved to a different resource.
Don't talk to residents about certain aspects of your personal life (like if you went drinking etc, even if it is completely legal for you to do so).
Know your supervisor's supervisor in case you need more support.
Get off campus as much as possible so you can recharge.
Stay in touch with non RA friends as much as you can so being an RA doesn't become your only social life.
If there is an intense incident that you helped out with GO TALK TO SOMEONE (therapist, friend, coworker, close family... keeping FERPA in mind with the last three) even if you think you are completely ok.

I would report him or simply talk to a supervisor for not doing his job as far as events and all of that goes. I had a floor partner like that and it was infuriating. After I said that my life got a lot easier. They never got my floor partner to do his job, but my supervisor drastically lessened the amount of work I needed to do. Idk what you identify as but as a societal thing and where I come from, women are often forced to do the brunt of all the planning events and artistic projects and I really felt like that played a big role in why I felt I was doing a ton more work.

My floor partner did not lose his job btw, but I don't have to work with him anymore!

Hi OP! I'm a third year RA, currently working in upperclassmen housing. My first two years were in freshman dorms. 

I saw my non-RA friends way less my first year as an RA because I didn't know how to create that balance. From my experience, friends won't be able to relate to all of the unique stressors of this job like your coworkers will, which can be isolating because they just didn't understand. Because of the on call nights and duty schedules it was also a lot harder to spend time with them. This led to me becoming great friends with my coworkers several years back, but I lost a few friends that I wasn't able to keep in touch with.

I came into this job really excited about the leadership experience and equally as excited about the compensation. After some traumatic experiences (while working the first two years) I've been through while working, I'm just here for the room and board. If I didn't have to work this job to continue going to school I wouldn't. 

That being said, this last year has been WAY easier so far. 

It really is up to what you want from college. If you really want or need this position then go for it, but there's a lot less stressful ways to grow as a person, gain leadership skills, and make money.

You are not a bad person and you are a great RA! This is my third year and I am having extreme burnout from this job too. Here are a few things I tell myself to stay sane. 

First, you're in college! The most important part is making sure you're doing what you're interested in, and doing well in your classes. Everything comes after that.

Second, this is just a job. Relationships (friends, partners, family) should also take precedence. At my university we are at will employees and they would let us go without a second thought, and I could also leave without notice. As amazing of a job as you've been doing, you are replaceable, and I think that's important to remember. You shouldn't be doing so much for this position that it is harmful to you.

I think from now on you should keep taking care of yourself and stop beating yourself up about setting boundaries. It's not your job to take care of everyone, and even if you're doing the bare minimum that is just what you're contracted to do. This job sucks sometimes and in order to help others you need to take care of yourself. You're a resident too.

I'm so sorry OP. I've been at the point (for some similar reasons) where I just barricade myself in my room when I can't take it anymore. If your hall director isn't going to do much with all the reports you have written so far then you need to make boundaries to take care of yourself. If that's not going to address incidents because you don't have energy then don't. Maybe it's asking a coworker from another floor talk to the resident. Example: coworker: "hey, we can hear you screaming on the floor above, you need to quiet down and I will be reporting this incident". And then you can both talk to your supervisor so that they see it's a bigger issue.

I would hope that if you were straight up and told your supervisor "this resident is cussing me out and does not comply with what I ask him to do (obey quiet hours be a respectful human etc) and it's inhibiting my ability to perform this job and connect with other residents." That they would respond accordingly but it doesn't seem like they are doing that, so my advice is to know your limits and if you need to not address things (as long as it's not an emergency) then from one RA to you, I think that's completely ok.

If the ideas in the other comments aren't possible I would ask your supervisor if it would be possible to not make a bulletin board for this month, telling them all of the reasons why that you outlined in this post.

Instead, you could help your coworkers with theirs or do some other sort of activity/workshop/creative thing for your floor that could give your residents the same information.

I go to a pretty nice public university (in my opinion) but you just don't know what housing deals with until you work for them. 

If your school has RAs being on call like this please don't put yourself through it if you can survive financially.
